stageFile.headline: French 101 Foundation private pilot
stageFile.threshold: Greet someone, use French articles and plurals, and ask simple questions.

lessons.title: Greetings and your name
lessons.objective: Greet a new adult learner, exchange names politely, and hear and produce the French /ʒ/, /u/, and nasal /ɔ̃/ sounds in familiar words.
lessons.focus: Greet someone with bonjour and introduce yourself with je m’appelle. The j in je and bonjour sounds /ʒ/; ou in bonjour sounds /u/; on in bonjour is a nasal vowel /ɔ̃/ with no separate n sound. Some final consonants are silent (Paris, salut), but others are pronounced (Marc, Paul, bonjour). Use vous with an adult you have just met; save tu for familiar classmates once you agree to be informal. A woman writes enchantée with a final -e; it sounds the same as enchanté.

words.en: pleased to meet you (said by a man)
pleased to meet you (said by a woman)

lessons.speaking: Role-play meeting another adult learner at a language café. Begin with Bonjour and Je m’appelle plus your name. Ask Comment vous appelez-vous ?; respond to Ça va ?; say Enchanté(e) and close with Merci, bonne journée ! and Au revoir. Your partner uses polite vous, repeats an unclear word, and explains unfamiliar words in English if asked. Then repeat bonjour and je m’appelle aloud, noticing /ʒ/, /u/, and nasal /ɔ̃/.

lessons.title: Masculine and feminine: le, la, un, une
lessons.objective: Name familiar classroom objects with un or une, and use le or la when pointing to a specific object.
lessons.focus: French nouns are grammatically masculine or feminine. Learn each object with its article: un stylo, une trousse. Use un/une when naming or introducing one object (C’est un cahier); use le/la for a particular object already identified (Voilà la gomme). The noun ending is only a partial gender clue, so learn the article with the noun. Hear the difference between nasal un and pronounced n in une, and between le and la.

words.en: And that one, is it a pencil case?

lessons.speaking: Role-play sorting objects with a classmate after class. Open with Qu’est-ce que c’est ? Name an unfamiliar object with C’est un... or C’est une..., then point to a specific known object with Voilà le... or Voilà la.... Ask whether another object is a stylo or a gomme and answer the same question. Close with Merci. Your partner gently checks the article and explains unfamiliar words in English when asked.

lessons.title: One thing or several: des, les and plurals
lessons.objective: Distinguish one classroom object from several using un/une/des and le/la/les, and hear plural meaning through the article.
lessons.focus: Most French plurals are written with -s: un crayon → des crayons. The final -s is usually silent, so the article often tells you whether one or several are meant: le /lə/ versus les /le/, un or une versus des /de/. Un and une become des for unspecified plural objects; le and la become les for specific plural objects. Nouns already ending in -s, -x, or -z keep that ending in the plural. Other patterns come later; learn each new plural in context.

words.es: Et ça, ce sont des stylos ?

lessons.speaking: Role-play sorting school supplies with a classmate. Open with Voilà les crayons. Ask whether another group consists of pens with Et ça, ce sont des stylos ? Point to a single eraser with Voilà la gomme, then identify the notebooks and books in the plural with les. Close with Merci and Au revoir. Your partner repeats an unclear article and explains unfamiliar words in English when asked.

lessons.title: Who is speaking?
lessons.objective: Introduce yourself and a classmate with je suis, tu es, and nous sommes; identify a third person or group with il/elle est or ils/elles sont, keeping tu or vous consistent with the relationship.
lessons.focus: Use être for “am / is / are”: je suis, tu es, il/elle est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils/elles sont. Peers often use tu right away; use vous with a teacher, staff member, or an adult stranger, and keep one register in a conversation. A mixed group uses ils, and masculine plural étudiants; an all-female group uses elles and étudiantes. In est the final t is usually silent, but it links before a vowel in il est ici; the t in êtes is pronounced.
lessons.speaking: Role-play meeting a classmate before class, using tu throughout. Opening: say Salut ! and ask Tu es plus the classmate’s name. Task 1: say who you are with Je suis plus your name, then ask Et toi, tu es ... ?. Task 2: say that you are both students with Nous sommes étudiants ici. Task 3: point to a teacher or classmate and say Il est là or Elle est là, matching that person, then point to a mixed group and say Ils sont étudiants for a mixed group (or Elles sont étudiantes for a group of women). Closure: say Merci and close with À demain ! Your partner uses tu throughout, repeats any unclear word, and explains unfamiliar words in English when asked.

lessons.title: Who am I? Identity and origin
lessons.objective: Introduce a learner’s role and origin with être and the appropriate Je viens de country chunk, and describe a person with a correctly matched adjective.
lessons.focus: Use être for roles and traits: je suis étudiant or étudiante; il est gentil, elle est gentille. A role normally has no article after être: je suis étudiante. Learn the noun or adjective ending for the person described. Learn Je viens de as a fixed origin chunk for now: de France for a feminine country, d’Espagne before a vowel, du Canada for a masculine country, and des États-Unis for a plural country. Country articles matter; do not apply de to every country.

Are you a student? (said to a man)
I come from the United States.

lessons.speaking: Role-play meeting another adult learner at a language café using vous throughout. Open with Bonjour and ask Vous êtes étudiant(e) ici ? State your role with Je suis étudiant or étudiante. Say your origin using one taught chunk: de France, d’Espagne, du Canada, or des États-Unis. If your country is different, ask the partner in English for its French form rather than guessing. Ask about a teacher and describe that person with il/elle est gentil/gentille or français/française. Close with Merci and Au revoir. Your partner uses vous and explains unfamiliar words in English when asked.

lessons.title: Where is it? Location and state
lessons.objective: Locate a person or object with être, sur, dans, or près de/du, and describe a state with an adjective that matches the noun or person.
lessons.focus: Use être for the locations and states in this lesson: Le livre est sur la table; La porte est ouverte. Some other everyday states use avoir (for example, j’ai faim); those come later. Sur means on, dans means in, and près de means near; before le, de + le becomes du (près du livre), and before les it becomes des (here meaning de + les, distinct from the indefinite article des). For a thing, il replaces a masculine noun and elle a feminine noun: le livre → il, la trousse → elle. Adjectives agree with the noun or person: le livre est ouvert, la porte est ouverte; Marc est fatigué, Claire est fatiguée.

words.en: Are you ready? (said to a woman)
It is on the table. (feminine noun)

lessons.speaking: Role-play finding objects in a classroom with an adult learner you have just met; use vous throughout. Open with Où est le stylo ? Answer using sur la table, dans la trousse, or près du livre (de + le → du). Ask where the trousse is and answer with Elle est... because trousse is feminine. Say Je suis fatigué/fatiguée and ask Vous êtes prêt/prête ? matching the person; then describe La porte est ouverte. Close with Merci and Au revoir. Your partner repeats unclear words and explains unfamiliar words in English when asked.
